title: Perioperative and cardiac surgical ICU
summary: Caring for the surgical patient in ICU: safe theatre handover and early complications, malignant hyperthermia and LAST, post-CABG and valve care, bleeding, tamponade and arrest after cardiac surgery (CALS), epicardial pacing, and frailty and obesity — with Indian practice notes.

topics.title: Post-operative handover and early complications
topics.summary: Taking a safe theatre-to-ICU handover, the first 30 minutes after arrival, and a systematic approach to the common early post-operative problems: hypoxaemia, hypotension, oliguria, hypothermia, pain, PONV, delirium and myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery (MINS).

definition.text: MINS (myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery) is a post-operative troponin elevation of presumed ischaemic origin, with or without symptoms, within 30 days of surgery. VISION 2017 defined it using hs-troponin T: peak 20 to <65 ng/L with an absolute change ≥5 ng/L, or any value ≥65 ng/L — each associated with increased 30-day mortality.

steps.title: Hands-off, eyes-on handover
steps.detail: Connect monitors and ventilator first, then stop everything for a structured handover with anaesthetist and surgeon present: patient and procedure, airway grade/difficulty, intra-operative events, blood loss, fluids/blood products, urine output, drugs given (antibiotic time, last opioid, reversal, vasopressors), lines/drains, and the explicit plan (BP target, analgesia, VTE, feeding, drains, when to call the surgeon).

steps.title: ABCDE assessment
steps.detail: Airway and breathing (SpO₂, RR, ETCO₂ if ventilated, chest expansion, residual neuromuscular block — TOF ratio <0.9 means incomplete reversal); circulation (MAP, HR, CRT, lactate, drains, wound); disability (pain score, sedation, pupils, glucose); exposure (temperature, pressure areas, limb perfusion).

steps.title: Baseline investigations
steps.detail: ABG with lactate, Hb, electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺), glucose, coagulation if bleeding risk, ECG; chest X-ray if central line, ETT, chest/abdominal procedure or hypoxaemia.

steps.title: Screen for myocardial injury (MINS)
steps.detail: In patients at risk (known cardiovascular disease, risk factors, age ≥65): troponin before and at 24 and 48 h after major surgery. Most MINS is silent — a rise needs ECG, review of haemodynamics/anaemia and cardiology input.

steps.title: Keep warm
steps.detail: Measure core temperature on arrival and hourly; if <36 °C use forced-air warming until ≥36.5 °C; warm IV fluids and blood above 500 mL.

steps.title: Analgesia and PONV
steps.detail: Multimodal analgesia (regular paracetamol, regional/epidural where placed, opioid-sparing adjuncts), pain score with every observation. PONV: assess Apfel risk factors (female, non-smoker, history of PONV/motion sickness, post-operative opioids); give 2 prophylactic agents for 1–2 risk factors and treat breakthrough with a different class.

steps.title: Prevent the predictable
steps.detail: VTE prophylaxis once haemostasis is secure; early mobilisation and feeding; delirium screening (CAM-ICU); glucose control; stop unnecessary lines and catheters; restart chronic medications appropriately (beta-blockers, statins).

redFlags.text: Hypotension with rising drain output, falling Hb or a tense abdomen = bleeding until proven otherwise: call the surgeon early.
New hypoxaemia after surgery: think atelectasis, residual neuromuscular block, opioid narcosis, aspiration, pneumothorax (after central line or thoracic surgery), pulmonary oedema and PE.
Chest pain, new ECG changes or troponin rise post-operatively are an ACS work-up, not a 'demand' explanation to ignore.
Fever, tachycardia, ileus or rising CRP on days 3–7 after bowel surgery: exclude anastomotic leak with CT.

pitfalls.text: Accepting a 'corridor handover' while moving the patient: information is lost; insist on a hands-off moment after monitoring is attached.
Treating post-operative hypertension with antihypertensives before treating pain, urinary retention or hypercapnia.
Giving the same antiemetic that failed as prophylaxis — use a different class.

pearls.text: Write the surgeon's 'call me if' criteria (drain output, MAP, Hb thresholds) on the chart at handover.
A rising lactate with a normal BP after major abdominal surgery may be the first sign of bleeding, ischaemic bowel or under-resuscitation.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Surgery triggers a stress response (catecholamines, cortisol, cytokines), hypercoagulability and fluid shifts. Anaesthetic drugs, opioids and residual neuromuscular block depress ventilation and airway reflexes; atelectasis develops in most patients after general anaesthesia. Supply–demand myocardial ischaemia (tachycardia, hypotension, anaemia) explains most MINS.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **ESC 2022 non-cardiac surgery guideline**: pre-operative risk assessment, peri-operative continuation of beta-blockers/statins in those already taking them, and recommendation to measure hs-troponin before and 24/48 h after intermediate/high-risk surgery in patients with cardiovascular disease, risk factors or age ≥65.
- **VISION (2017)**: 21,842 patients; hs-troponin T thresholds associated with 30-day mortality; MINS mostly asymptomatic (>90% without ischaemic symptoms).
- **Fourth Consensus Guidelines on PONV (2020)**: risk-based multimodal prophylaxis; avoid using the same drug class for rescue.
- **NICE CG65**: measure temperature, keep ≥36 °C, forced-air warming.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Routine troponin screening: improves detection, but the best treatment of MINS is uncertain (MANAGE trial suggested benefit of dabigatran).
- Liberal vs restrictive peri-operative fluids (RELIEF: restrictive associated with more AKI).
- Target BP after surgery — individualised (e.g. within 10–20% of baseline) vs fixed MAP 65.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Many Indian patients arrive in ICU from theatres in other blocks without the anaesthetist; insist on a phone/face-to-face handover and a written anaesthesia chart.
- Forced-air warming devices may be limited; warmed fluids, blankets and room temperature control still help.
- hs-troponin may not be available everywhere; conventional troponin trends plus ECG are acceptable.
- Post-operative delirium is under-recognised in Indian wards; routine CAM-ICU screening is low cost.

topics.title: Malignant hyperthermia and local anaesthetic systemic toxicity
topics.summary: Two rare but lethal anaesthetic emergencies that can present in theatre, recovery or ICU: malignant hyperthermia (stop triggers, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg, cool, treat hyperkalaemia) and LAST (airway, seizure control, 20% lipid emulsion, modified ACLS).

definition.text: Malignant hyperthermia is a pharmacogenetic (usually RYR1 or CACNA1S variant) disorder of skeletal muscle calcium handling triggered by volatile anaesthetics and suxamethonium, causing hypermetabolism. LAST is toxicity from high plasma local anaesthetic concentrations affecting the CNS and heart (sodium-channel blockade).

steps.title: Suspect malignant hyperthermia
steps.detail: During/after volatile anaesthetic or suxamethonium: unexplained rising ETCO₂ despite increased ventilation, tachycardia, masseter or generalised rigidity, mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis, hyperkalaemia, arrhythmias; hyperthermia is often LATE. Can appear up to hours after exposure.

steps.title: Stop triggers, call for help, hyperventilate
steps.detail: Stop volatile agents and suxamethonium; declare an MH emergency and get the MH kit/dantrolene; 100% O₂ at high fresh-gas flow (≥10 L/min); hyperventilate (2–3 × minute volume); insert activated charcoal filters if available; switch to TIVA if surgery must continue; tell the surgeon to finish quickly.

steps.title: Dantrolene
steps.detail: 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus (each 20 mg vial needs 60 mL sterile water — assign several people to reconstitute). Repeat every 5–10 min until ETCO₂, HR and temperature settle; most need ≤10 mg/kg but give more if signs persist.

steps.title: Cool and treat complications
steps.detail: If temperature >39 °C: cold IV saline, surface cooling, ice packs to groin/axillae; stop cooling at ~38.5 °C. Hyperkalaemia: insulin–glucose, calcium, hyperventilation. Arrhythmias: amiodarone or beta-blocker; avoid calcium-channel blockers with dantrolene. Aim urine output ≥2 mL/kg/h (fluids, consider furosemide) to protect against myoglobinuric AKI.

steps.title: ICU for ≥24 h
steps.detail: Monitor for recrudescence: continue dantrolene 1 mg/kg every 4–6 h (or infusion) for 24 h; check CK, K⁺, myoglobin, coagulation (DIC), renal function. Refer patient and family for MH susceptibility testing (contracture testing/genetic) and give an alert card.

steps.title: Suspect local anaesthetic systemic toxicity
steps.detail: Within seconds to ~1 h of a block, infiltration or IV lidocaine: perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, agitation, confusion, seizures, then bradycardia, wide-QRS arrhythmias, hypotension, cardiac arrest (may be the first sign, especially with bupivacaine).

steps.title: Stop, call, airway
steps.detail: Stop injecting; call for help and the LAST kit; 100% O₂, ventilate to prevent hypoxia and acidosis; treat seizures with a benzodiazepine (avoid large doses of propofol in cardiovascular instability).

steps.title: Lipid emulsion 20%
steps.detail: At the first sign of serious toxicity: >70 kg give 100 mL over 2–3 min then 200–250 mL over 15–20 min; ≤70 kg give 1.5 mL/kg bolus then 0.25 mL/kg/min. Repeat bolus once or twice and/or double infusion if still unstable; upper limit ~12 mL/kg.

steps.title: Modified ACLS
steps.detail: Small adrenaline doses (≤1 mcg/kg); avoid vasopressin, calcium-channel blockers, beta-blockers and local anaesthetics (lidocaine/procainamide) for arrhythmias; prolonged CPR — consider cardiopulmonary bypass/ECMO if available. Monitor ≥4–6 h after cardiovascular toxicity (≥2 h after isolated CNS signs).

redFlags.text: Unexplained rising ETCO₂ with tachycardia under volatile anaesthesia = MH until proven otherwise; temperature rise is a late sign.
Masseter spasm after suxamethonium is an early warning of MH susceptibility — stop volatile agents and monitor closely.
Bupivacaine cardiotoxicity can present as cardiac arrest without preceding seizures; start lipid immediately.
Do not use propofol as a lipid source: its lipid content is too low and the drug causes cardiovascular depression.

pitfalls.text: Dissolving dantrolene in saline or dextrose — it precipitates; use sterile water and warm it if possible.
Calcium-channel blockers with dantrolene can cause severe hyperkalaemia and cardiovascular collapse.
Stopping resuscitation early in LAST: recovery can occur after prolonged CPR with lipid; arrange ECMO/bypass early.

pearls.text: Keep a laminated MH and LAST checklist (and the lipid bag) wherever regional blocks or volatile anaesthetics are used — including ICU, labour ward and procedure rooms.
Calculate the total local anaesthetic dose (including surgeon infiltration) at the time-out for big blocks.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: In MH, abnormal ryanodine receptors release excess Ca²⁺ from sarcoplasmic reticulum, causing sustained muscle contraction, ATP depletion, CO₂ and heat production, rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia. Dantrolene blocks RYR1 Ca²⁺ release. LAST: sodium-channel blockade in brain (excitation then depression) and heart (conduction block, reduced contractility); lipid emulsion acts as a 'sink' and provides direct cardiotonic/metabolic effects.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **EMHG 2010 guideline** and **MHAUS** crisis protocol: immediate trigger removal, hyperventilation with high fresh-gas flow, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg repeated, active cooling, management of hyperkalaemia and arrhythmias, and post-crisis monitoring and referral.
- Dantrolene introduction reduced MH mortality from historical figures of ~70–80% to under 5–10% in centres with prompt treatment.
- **ASRA LAST checklist 2020**: lipid emulsion dosing simplified by weight (>70 kg fixed 100 mL bolus), modified ACLS (small adrenaline doses), prolonged monitoring.
- Lipid emulsion evidence is from animal studies, case series and registries; no RCTs are feasible.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- How much dantrolene to stock in hospitals with infrequent volatile use (cost vs risk).
- Lipid emulsion for non-local-anaesthetic lipophilic drug overdose (e.g. some calcium-channel blockers) — weak evidence, interferes with lab tests and ECMO circuits.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Dantrolene is expensive and often not stocked in Indian hospitals; many units rely on borrowing from nearby centres — know your nearest supply in advance. MH-susceptibility testing (contracture tests) is not widely available in India; genetic testing may be accessible through private laboratories.
- Suxamethonium and halothane/isoflurane remain widely used in India, so MH can present anywhere, including district hospitals.
- Lipid emulsion 20% is usually stocked as parenteral nutrition in pharmacy — keep a dedicated bag in theatre/LAST kit.
- Ultrasound-guided blocks by surgeons and in emergency departments increase LAST exposure outside theatres.

topics.title: Post-CABG and valve surgery care
topics.summary: The first 24 hours after cardiac surgery: arrival bundle, haemodynamic and metabolic targets, early extubation, recognising low cardiac output syndrome versus vasoplegia, post-operative AF, transfusion thresholds and valve-specific points.

definition.text: Low cardiac output syndrome (LCOS) after cardiac surgery is commonly defined as cardiac index <2.2 L/min/m² with signs of hypoperfusion despite adequate filling, requiring inotropes or mechanical support. Vasoplegia is hypotension with low systemic vascular resistance and preserved or high cardiac output after cardiopulmonary bypass.

steps.title: Arrival bundle
steps.detail: Attach monitoring (ECG, arterial line, CVP ± PA catheter, SpO₂, ETCO₂), check pacing box connections and settings, label and check drains, take structured handover (procedure, bypass/cross-clamp times, grafts/valve, weaning difficulty, inotropes, protamine given, TOE findings, bleeding). ABG, Hb, K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, glucose, lactate, ACT/coagulation, ECG and chest X-ray.

steps.title: Haemodynamic targets
steps.detail: Typical targets (individualise with the surgeon): MAP 65–80 mmHg (avoid hypertension — suture-line bleeding), HR 80–100/min (pace if needed), cardiac index >2.2 L/min/m², ScvO₂ >65%, lactate falling, urine >0.5 mL/kg/h.

steps.title: Rewarm, ventilate, extubate early
steps.detail: Rewarm to normothermia but avoid >37.5 °C; lung-protective ventilation; aim for extubation within 6 h when warm, awake, not bleeding and haemodynamically stable.

steps.title: Electrolytes and glucose
steps.detail: Keep K⁺ 4.0–5.0 mmol/L and Mg²⁺ ≥1 mmol/L (reduces arrhythmia); glucose <180 mg/dL (10 mmol/L) with an insulin infusion protocol, avoiding hypoglycaemia.

steps.title: Bleeding and transfusion
steps.detail: Monitor drain output hourly; keep tubes patent without stripping. Restrictive red-cell transfusion (Hb <7.5 g/dL) is non-inferior in moderate–high-risk cardiac surgery (TRICS III), unless active bleeding or ischaemia.

steps.title: Low cardiac output vs vasoplegia
steps.detail: Low BP + low CI + cold peripheries + rising lactate = low cardiac output syndrome: check rhythm/rate, preload, tamponade (echo/TOE), graft ischaemia (ECG), RV failure; then inotrope (dobutamine/milrinone/adrenaline), IABP or MCS. Low BP + normal/high CI + warm = vasoplegia: noradrenaline, then vasopressin, then methylene blue rescue (not in G6PD deficiency).

steps.title: Post-operative AF
steps.detail: Occurs in ~20–40% after cardiac surgery, peaking day 2–3. Continue/restart beta-blockers when stable; correct K⁺/Mg²⁺; rate or rhythm control (beta-blocker, amiodarone); DC cardioversion if unstable; consider anticoagulation if AF persists >48 h, balancing surgical bleeding risk.

steps.title: Recovery bundle
steps.detail: Multimodal analgesia; delirium screening; early mobilisation; restart statin and antiplatelet therapy per surgical protocol; VTE prophylaxis once bleeding settled; AKI prevention (avoid nephrotoxins, maintain perfusion).

redFlags.text: Falling BP with rising CVP and a sudden fall in drain output = tamponade until proven otherwise — call the surgeon immediately.
New ST changes, VF or regional wall-motion abnormality after CABG suggests graft failure — urgent surgeon/cardiology review (angiography).
Lactate rising above 4 mmol/L despite targets = inadequate delivery: reassess cardiac output, Hb, bleeding and abdomen (mesenteric ischaemia).
Avoid hypertension (SBP >140 mmHg) in the early hours: it increases bleeding from anastomoses.

pitfalls.text: Treating low BP with escalating noradrenaline without measuring cardiac output: vasoconstriction worsens low-output states — get an echo.
Allowing K⁺ to fall below 4 mmol/L in the first 24 h after bypass: high diuresis drives hypokalaemia and arrhythmias.
Stripping or milking chest drains, or breaking the sterile system to clear clots: not recommended; maintain patency by safe techniques.

pearls.text: Pacing at 80–90/min (AAI/DDD) is often the simplest 'inotrope' for a stiff, recently arrested heart.
Beta-blocker restart (when off inotropes) is the most effective measure to reduce post-operative AF.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Cardiopulmonary bypass causes systemic inflammation, haemodilution, platelet dysfunction and fibrinolysis, myocardial stunning after cross-clamping (typical nadir of function 4–6 h post-op), and vasoplegia via nitric oxide and vasopressin deficiency. Diuresis after bypass shifts K⁺ and Mg²⁺. Post-operative AF arises from atrial inflammation, sympathetic activation and electrolyte shifts.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **ERAS Cardiac Society 2019**: recommendations include perioperative glycaemic control (insulin infusion to <180 mg/dL), goal-directed fluid therapy, chest-tube patency without stripping, early extubation (<6 h), prevention of hyperthermia on rewarming, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, delirium screening, AKI risk mitigation and pharmacological thromboprophylaxis.
- **TRICS III (2017):** 5,243 moderate-to-high-risk cardiac surgery patients; restrictive threshold (Hb <7.5 g/dL) non-inferior to liberal (<9.5 ICU / <8.5 ward) for death, MI, stroke and new dialysis; fewer transfusions.
- **2023 ACC/AHA AF guideline:** post-operative AF after cardiac surgery is common, associated with stroke and mortality; beta-blockers for prevention, amiodarone prophylaxis in high-risk patients, and anticoagulation considered for persistent POAF when bleeding risk allows.
- **EACTS/EACTA/EBCP CPB guideline 2019:** management of bypass-related physiology including vasoplegia.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Routine PA catheter use (declining; echo increasingly preferred).
- Levosimendan in LCOS (LEVO-CTS, LICORN, CHEETAH trials were neutral).
- Early vs delayed anticoagulation for POAF after cardiac surgery.
- Methylene blue for vasoplegia — signal of benefit in observational data only.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- India performs a very large volume of CABG (many off-pump) with shorter ICU stays; off-pump patients have less vasoplegia and bleeding but similar AF.
- Rheumatic heart disease remains a major indication for valve surgery in India: mitral stenosis/regurgitation with pulmonary hypertension and AF, often young patients; mechanical valves with warfarin are common, so INR monitoring access and adherence counselling matter.
- **G6PD deficiency** prevalence is significant in parts of India — methylene blue can cause severe haemolysis; check status where possible.
- Government schemes (PM-JAY and state schemes) cover many cardiac surgeries; ICU resources may be stretched, making early extubation and fast-track protocols important.

topics.title: Bleeding, tamponade and cardiac arrest after cardiac surgery
topics.summary: Distinguishing surgical from coagulopathic bleeding, a targeted (viscoelastic-guided) correction bundle, when to call for re-exploration, recognising post-operative tamponade, and the cardiac-surgery-specific arrest protocol (CALS/STS: three shocks, pace, resternotomy within 5 minutes).

definition.text: Excessive bleeding after cardiac surgery results from surgical sources and/or coagulopathy (residual heparin, platelet dysfunction, haemodilution, fibrinolysis, hypothermia). Re-exploration occurs in roughly 2–6% of patients and is associated with higher mortality — mostly when delayed.

steps.title: Measure bleeding
steps.detail: Record drain output every hour (more often if heavy); check for clots in tubing, Hb, ACT, platelet count, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, ionised calcium, temperature and, where available, TEG/ROTEM.

steps.title: Basics: warm, calcium, pressure
steps.detail: Normothermia (≥36 °C), ionised calcium >1.1 mmol/L, pH >7.2, avoid hypertension (agree a lower SBP/MAP target with the surgeon), PEEP may be modestly increased only with surgeon agreement.

steps.title: Correct coagulopathy
steps.detail: Residual heparin (ACT prolonged / heparinase test): protamine 25–50 mg slow IV. Fibrinogen <1.5 g/L: cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate. Platelets <50–100 × 10⁹/L or antiplatelet drugs: platelets ± desmopressin 0.3 mcg/kg. Prolonged clotting times: FFP or prothrombin complex concentrate. Tranexamic acid if hyperfibrinolysis or per protocol.

steps.title: Call the surgeon early
steps.detail: Re-exploration is usually considered for heavy ongoing bleeding (commonly quoted: >400 mL in the first hour, >200 mL/h for 2–4 h, or sudden increase) despite correction, or any haemodynamic compromise/tamponade. Do not 'chase' surgical bleeding with blood products alone.

steps.title: Recognise post-operative tamponade
steps.detail: Hypotension, tachycardia (or loss of pacing response), rising CVP and filling pressures, falling cardiac output/urine, rising lactate, widening mediastinum, sudden drop in drain output (clotted tubes). Can be LOCALISED (clot over right atrium/ventricle) with atypical echo — TOE if transthoracic views are poor.

steps.title: Three stacked shocks first
steps.detail: Witnessed VF/pVT in a monitored post-cardiac-surgery patient: up to 3 rapid successive shocks (within ~1 min) BEFORE external compressions; amiodarone 300 mg after the third failed shock.

steps.title: Pace first
steps.detail: Asystole or extreme bradycardia: if pacing wires present, pace DDD at 80–100/min at maximum output before starting CPR; atropine 1 mg if no wires.

steps.title: Turn off pacing, think tamponade
steps.detail: PEA: pause pacing to exclude underlying VF; start CPR; hypovolaemia/tamponade/tension pneumothorax are likely. Avoid full-dose adrenaline (1 mg) — consider small doses only on senior advice.

steps.title: Emergency resternotomy
steps.detail: If no ROSC after the above, prepare for emergency resternotomy within 5 minutes (within ~10 days of surgery) — the resternotomy kit should be in the ICU; six key roles (compressions, airway, defibrillation, team leader, drugs, ICU coordinator).

redFlags.text: Drain output suddenly stops in a bleeding patient who becomes hypotensive = clotted drains and tamponade, not 'bleeding has stopped'.
Hypotension with high CVP after cardiac surgery: tamponade, RV failure or tension pneumothorax — echo and call the surgeon.
External chest compressions in a fresh sternotomy can cause cardiac/graft injury: shocks or pacing first, but do not delay CPR beyond ~1 minute.
Massive bleeding (>1.5 L in 1 h or haemodynamic instability) — activate massive transfusion protocol and inform theatre.

pitfalls.text: Giving blind 'shotgun' FFP and platelets without tests: increases transfusion-related harm and delays recognition of surgical bleeding.
Excess protamine: protamine itself impairs coagulation and can cause hypotension and pulmonary hypertension.
Waiting for a full transthoracic echo to diagnose tamponade in a peri-arrest patient: clinical suspicion is enough to call for re-opening.

pearls.text: Write the 'call the surgeon' bleeding threshold on the observation chart at handover so nurses escalate without debate.
Check the pacing box and wires as part of every post-op arrest: pacing failure is a reversible cause.

algorithm.title: Arrest after cardiac surgery (CALS/STS)
algorithm.description: Modified ALS for monitored patients after cardiac surgery.

Rhythm?
Up to 3 stacked shocks within 1 min

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Tamponade after cardiac surgery is often caused by clot rather than free fluid; the open pericardium allows localised compression of a single chamber (commonly the right atrium or right ventricle), so classical signs (equalisation of pressures, pulsus paradoxus) may be absent. Coagulopathy after bypass reflects heparin, haemodilution, platelet activation/consumption on the circuit and fibrinolysis.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **EACTS/EACTA 2017 Patient Blood Management guideline**: pre-operative anaemia management, antifibrinolytics, viscoelastic-guided transfusion algorithms (IIa), fibrinogen/PCC use, restrictive thresholds, and protamine dosing.
- **STS 2017 expert consensus** (building on **EACTS 2009** guideline): for arrest after cardiac surgery, three sequential shocks before compressions for VF/VT, immediate pacing for asystole/bradycardia, early emergency resternotomy (within 5 min) and avoidance of routine 1 mg adrenaline; resuscitation teams train with CALS (Cardiac Surgical Advanced Life Support).
- Survival after arrest following cardiac surgery is much higher than in other in-hospital arrests (often quoted around 50%) because causes are frequently reversible (tamponade, bleeding, graft occlusion, arrhythmia).
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Fixed volume thresholds vs clinical judgment for re-exploration.
- Fibrinogen concentrate vs cryoprecipitate (FIBRES trial: non-inferior).
- Prophylactic tranexamic acid dose (OPTIMAL trial: high vs low dose — high dose reduced transfusion, seizure risk similar in that trial).
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Fibrinogen concentrate and PCC are costly and not universally stocked in India — cryoprecipitate is the usual source of fibrinogen; know your blood bank's turnaround time.
- TEG/ROTEM is available mostly in large cardiac centres; standard lab coagulation tests and clinical judgment are used elsewhere.
- Every cardiac surgical ICU should have a sterile resternotomy pack and a CALS-trained team at the bedside 24/7.

topics.title: Epicardial pacing wires and temporary pacing
topics.summary: How to read and set a temporary pacing box after cardiac surgery: modes (AAI, VVI, DDD, asynchronous), output and sensitivity thresholds, daily checks, troubleshooting failure to capture or sense, and safe wire removal.

definition.text: Temporary epicardial wires are stitched to the atrial and/or ventricular epicardium at the end of cardiac surgery to treat bradyarrhythmias, optimise cardiac output (AV synchrony, rate) and terminate some tachyarrhythmias. Their thresholds rise over days because of inflammation and fibrosis, and many fail by day 4–5.

steps.title: Identify the wires
steps.detail: Confirm which wires are atrial and which ventricular (by convention atrial often exit right of the sternum and ventricular left — but always check the operation note/labels). Connect to the pacing box with labelled cables; keep unused wires insulated and dry.

steps.title: Record the settings
steps.detail: Document mode, rate, atrial and ventricular output (mA), sensitivity (mV), AV delay and underlying rhythm on the chart. Check the box battery and have a spare battery and transcutaneous pacing pads available.

steps.title: Select the mode
steps.detail: Sinus bradycardia with intact AV conduction → AAI. AF/flutter with slow ventricular response → VVI. Heart block with atrial activity → DDD. Asynchronous (AOO/VOO/DOO) only temporarily (e.g. diathermy interference) — risk of R-on-T VF.

steps.title: Threshold testing
steps.detail: Capture threshold: at a rate above intrinsic, reduce output until capture is lost; set output at least 2–3 × threshold. Sensing threshold: set rate below intrinsic, increase the mV number until sensing fails (pacing spikes appear); set sensitivity at about half that value. Do NOT test capture in pacing-dependent patients without senior help.

steps.title: Failure to capture
steps.detail: Spikes without P/QRS: increase output, check connections and battery, reverse polarity, correct K⁺/acidosis/ischaemia; if wires failing, use a skin needle as an indifferent electrode (unipolar), start transcutaneous pacing or isoprenaline, arrange transvenous pacing.

steps.title: Failure to sense / oversensing
steps.detail: Undersensing (inappropriate spikes on intrinsic beats; risk of R-on-T): make more sensitive (lower mV). Oversensing (pauses because noise/T-waves inhibit pacing; crosstalk in DDD): make less sensitive, check leads, shorten ventricular blanking per expert advice.

steps.title: Overdrive pacing (expert)
steps.detail: Type 1 atrial flutter post-op may be terminated by rapid atrial pacing via atrial wires (e.g. 10–20% above flutter rate) — only with ventricular wire backup and senior/cardiology supervision; never deliver rapid pacing through ventricular wires.

steps.title: Removal
steps.detail: Remove when no longer needed (often day 3–5, before discharge). Check INR, platelets and that heparin/LMWH is timed appropriately; pull gently with steady traction (cut flush at skin if resistant, per surgeon). Bed rest and monitor BP/HR for ~1 h; watch for tamponade.

redFlags.text: Pacing-dependent patient (no underlying rhythm): never switch off or disconnect for testing without transcutaneous pacing ready.
Spikes falling on T-waves (undersensing) can trigger VF — fix sensitivity or switch off pacing if the intrinsic rhythm is adequate.
Hypotension and tachycardia after wire removal = tamponade until proven otherwise: echo and call the surgeon.

pitfalls.text: Handling exposed wire tips with ungloved hands or leaving them in contact with metal: microshocks can induce VF.
Forgetting that a pacing box set to asynchronous mode during surgery is still in DOO on ICU arrival — check and change to a demand mode.
Removing wires while the patient is fully anticoagulated (high INR or just after LMWH dose).

pearls.text: AV-sequential pacing (DDD/DVI) can improve cardiac output by 15–20% compared with VVI in stiff post-operative ventricles that depend on the atrial kick.
Atrial electrogram (connect atrial wires to a precordial ECG lead) helps diagnose wide- or narrow-complex tachycardia after surgery.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Epicardial electrodes sense and stimulate local myocardium; the capture threshold rises with local oedema, inflammation and fibrosis, plus metabolic factors (acidosis, hyperkalaemia, ischaemia, antiarrhythmic drugs). The post-operative ventricle is stiff and benefits from AV synchrony and a higher rate (80–90/min) to maintain cardiac output.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **Reade 2007 (two-part practical review, Anaesthesia)**: indications, wire placement, pacing codes, mode selection, threshold testing, troubleshooting, overdrive pacing for atrial flutter and removal complications.
- Bradyarrhythmias requiring pacing are commonest after valve surgery (especially aortic and tricuspid) because of proximity of the conduction system; persistent complete heart block beyond ~5–7 days usually needs a permanent pacemaker.
- Complications of wire removal (bleeding, tamponade, arrhythmia, retained wire) are uncommon but potentially fatal.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Routine placement of wires in all patients vs selective (e.g. omitted in uncomplicated CABG in some centres).
- Optimal timing of removal relative to anticoagulation for mechanical valves.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Temporary pacing boxes may be shared between ICU beds in Indian units; label each box with the patient, mode and thresholds and charge/replace batteries per schedule.
- Transvenous pacing expertise is typically in cardiology on call; agree escalation pathways in advance.
- Rheumatic and congenital valve surgery in young Indian patients leads to frequent conduction problems post-op.

topics.title: Frailty and obesity in the surgical ICU patient
topics.summary: Assessing frailty with the Clinical Frailty Scale and using it to shape goals and post-operative care, and the practical ICU management of the obese surgical patient: weight scalars for drug dosing, airway and ventilation, OSA, VTE and pressure care.

definition.text: Frailty is a state of reduced physiological reserve and increased vulnerability to stressors; the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) is a judgment-based 9-point scale (extended from the original 7-point scale validated in 2005). Obesity is BMI ≥30 kg/m² (WHO), but WHO suggests lower action points (23 and 27.5 kg/m²) for Asian populations.

steps.title: Score frailty
steps.detail: Record the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) based on the patient's function 2 weeks BEFORE the acute illness (ask family). CFS ≥5 = frail. Use it to inform discussions and care planning, not as a sole triage tool.

steps.title: Frailty-focused care
steps.detail: Goals-of-care conversation early with patient and family; delirium prevention (orientation, sleep, glasses/hearing aids, avoid benzodiazepines/anticholinergics); careful fluid and drug dosing (low muscle mass — creatinine overestimates GFR); early mobilisation and nutrition; review polypharmacy.

steps.title: Measure and calculate weights
steps.detail: Measure actual (total) body weight and height; calculate BMI, predicted (ideal) body weight, lean body weight and adjusted body weight. Asian populations have higher metabolic risk at lower BMI.

steps.title: Airway and extubation
steps.detail: Expect difficult mask ventilation and rapid desaturation: ramped/head-up position, preoxygenate with CPAP/HFNC, videolaryngoscope. Extubate fully awake and sitting up; apply HFNC or CPAP early after extubation, especially with known/suspected OSA.

steps.title: Lung-protective ventilation
steps.detail: Set tidal volume by predicted body weight (6–8 mL/kg PBW), not actual weight; use higher PEEP (often 8–12 cmH₂O or titrated) and head-up 30–45° to counter atelectasis; consider recruitment if haemodynamically stable.

steps.title: Choose the right weight scalar
steps.detail: Lipophilic induction agents and opioids by lean body weight; propofol infusion by total or adjusted weight; suxamethonium by total weight; rocuronium by ideal/lean weight; titrate to effect and monitor (TOF, BIS if available). Antibiotics and LMWH often need higher doses — check local protocol.

steps.title: VTE, pressure areas, rhabdomyolysis
steps.detail: Weight-adjusted VTE prophylaxis plus mechanical methods; bariatric beds and appropriately sized cuffs; check pressure areas and CK after long surgery (gluteal rhabdomyolysis); screen and treat OSA with CPAP; glucose control.

doseCards.dose: 15 mg/kg every 6 h if <50 kg (max 60 mg/kg/day, ≤3 g/day if hepatic risk)

redFlags.text: Frail patients often present atypically: delirium, falls or 'off legs' may be the only sign of sepsis or a surgical complication.
Obese patient desaturating after extubation: sit up, CPAP/HFNC, check residual neuromuscular block and opioid excess — re-intubation is high-risk.
Severe gluteal or back pain, dark urine and rising CK after prolonged surgery in an obese patient = rhabdomyolysis; check compartments and renal function.

pitfalls.text: Setting tidal volume on actual weight in an obese patient (e.g. 8 mL/kg × 120 kg = 960 mL) — volutrauma; use PBW.
Using serum creatinine alone to judge renal function in frail, sarcopenic patients — it overestimates GFR; dose renally cleared drugs cautiously.
Labelling a patient 'frail' from their acute ICU state rather than baseline function.

pearls.text: Ask the family: 'Two weeks before this illness, what could they do on their own?' — this one question gives most of the CFS.
A ramp (ear level with sternum) and 25–30° head-up improves both laryngoscopy view and FRC in obese patients.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Frailty reflects cumulative deficits across systems (sarcopenia, reduced cardiorespiratory and immune reserve, cognitive vulnerability). Obesity reduces FRC and chest-wall compliance, increases oxygen consumption, promotes atelectasis and OSA, and alters drug distribution (lipophilic drugs distribute into fat; hydrophilic drugs mostly into lean mass).
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **Rockwood 2005 (CSHA, CMAJ)**: Clinical Frailty Scale correlated with the frailty index and predicted death and institutionalisation; now extended to 9 points (version 2.0, 2020).
- Frailty in ICU patients is consistently associated with higher mortality, longer stay, delirium and discharge to institutional care; it should inform but not replace individual decisions.
- **ESC 2022 non-cardiac surgery guideline** highlights frailty assessment in older surgical patients as part of risk evaluation.
- **AAGBI/SOBA 2015**: obese surgical patient guidance — 'obesity paradox', weight scalars, airway management, OSA, regional anaesthesia, post-operative monitoring and VTE.
- **STOP-BANG (Chung 2008)**: simple OSA screening; high sensitivity at a score ≥3.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Use of frailty scores in ICU triage or rationing (risk of discrimination; best used alongside individual assessment).
- 'Obesity paradox' in critical illness — lower observed mortality in mildly obese ICU patients may reflect confounding.
- Optimal PEEP strategy in obese patients (PROBESE: higher PEEP + recruitment did not reduce pulmonary complications).
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- India's ageing population and rising obesity/diabetes ('thin-fat' phenotype with central adiposity at lower BMI) mean frailty and metabolic disease frequently coexist in surgical ICUs.
- Indian consensus guidance commonly classifies overweight as BMI 23–24.9 and obesity as ≥25 kg/m² (aligned with WHO Asian action points) — verify current national guidance.
- OSA is widely under-diagnosed in India; STOP-BANG at pre-op and ICU admission is cheap and useful.
- Bariatric beds, large BP cuffs and lifting equipment may be scarce — plan before elective bariatric or major surgery.

drugs.name: Dantrolene sodium
drugs.class: Ryanodine receptor (RYR1) antagonist; skeletal muscle relaxant
drugs.adultDose: 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus as fast as possible; repeat 1 mg/kg (or 2.5 mg/kg per MHAUS) every 5–10 min until hypermetabolism resolves; usual total up to 10 mg/kg, more if still needed. Then 1 mg/kg every 4–6 h (or 0.25 mg/kg/h infusion) for 24 h to prevent recrudescence.
drugs.preparationIndia: Classic vials: 20 mg dantrolene + 3 g mannitol, each reconstituted with 60 mL sterile water (not saline/dextrose) — slow to dissolve; assign several people. Newer 250 mg/5 mL formulation (Ryanodex) dissolves fast but is rarely available in India. MHAUS recommends 36 × 20 mg vials stocked where triggering agents are used.
drugs.cautions: Thrombophlebitis (large vein); muscle weakness; avoid with calcium-channel blockers (hyperkalaemia, myocardial depression). Mannitol content causes diuresis.
drugs.monitoring: ETCO₂, temperature, K⁺, CK, myoglobinuria, ABG, urine output.
drugs.verify: Indian availability and stocking: many hospitals do not hold dantrolene; confirm local stock and the nearest supply point.

drugs.name: Lipid emulsion 20% (intravenous fat emulsion)
drugs.indications: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) with significant cardiovascular or neurological toxicity
drugs.adultDose: >70 kg: 100 mL bolus over 2–3 min, then 200–250 mL over 15–20 min. ≤70 kg: 1.5 mL/kg (lean body weight) bolus over 2–3 min, then 0.25 mL/kg/min. If still unstable: repeat bolus once or twice and/or double infusion rate. Upper limit about 12 mL/kg.
drugs.preparationIndia: 20% soya-based lipid emulsions (100 mL, 250 mL, 500 mL bags) are available as parenteral nutrition products; keep one in theatre and in the LAST kit. Propofol is NOT a substitute.
drugs.cautions: Lipaemia interferes with lab tests; pancreatitis, fat overload with excess doses.
drugs.monitoring: ECG, BP, neurological status; continue monitoring ≥4–6 h after a cardiovascular event (≥2 h after seizure only).

drugs.name: Protamine sulfate
drugs.indications: Reversal of residual heparin after cardiopulmonary bypass ('heparin rebound') or heparin overdose
drugs.adultDose: 1 mg neutralises ~100 units of heparin. After CPB, top-up doses typically 25–50 mg slow IV guided by ACT/heparin assay; give slowly (≤5 mg/min); single dose ≤50 mg.
drugs.preparationIndia: 10 mg/mL ampoules (5 mL = 50 mg) commonly available.
drugs.cautions: Hypotension, anaphylaxis, catastrophic pulmonary hypertension (risk: fish allergy, protamine-insulin use, vasectomy, prior exposure). Excess protamine is itself anticoagulant.
drugs.monitoring: ACT, aPTT, BP, pulmonary artery pressure if available.

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid
drugs.indications: Prevention/treatment of bleeding in cardiac surgery and post-operative haemorrhage
drugs.adultDose: Cardiac surgery protocols vary: commonly 10–30 mg/kg IV load with or without infusion; for post-operative bleeding 1 g IV over 10 min (may repeat). Reduce in renal impairment.
drugs.preparationIndia: 500 mg/5 mL ampoules widely available and cheap.
drugs.renalHepatic: Renally excreted: reduce dose in AKI.
drugs.cautions: Seizures (dose-related, especially high-dose regimens in open-chamber surgery), thrombosis.
drugs.verify: Exact cardiac-surgery dosing regimen per local anaesthesia protocol.

drugs.name: Desmopressin (DDAVP)
drugs.class: Vasopressin V2 analogue; releases von Willebrand factor/factor VIII
drugs.indications: Bleeding with platelet dysfunction (antiplatelet drugs, uraemia, von Willebrand disease) after cardiac surgery
drugs.adultDose: 0.3 mcg/kg IV in 50 mL saline over 20–30 min (single dose; tachyphylaxis with repeats).
drugs.cautions: Hypotension if given fast, hyponatraemia, thrombosis.

drugs.name: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine)
drugs.indications: Vasoplegia after cardiopulmonary bypass; post-operative hypotension with adequate filling
drugs.adultDose: 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min IV infusion titrated to MAP (often 65–80 mmHg after cardiac surgery per surgeon).
drugs.preparationIndia: 2 mg/2 mL ampoules (check base vs bitartrate labelling); 4 mg in 50 mL = 80 mcg/mL; 8 mg in 50 mL = 160 mcg/mL.
drugs.cautions: Extravasation; excess afterload on a failing LV; mesenteric/digital ischaemia at high doses.
drugs.monitoring: Arterial line, lactate, urine output, cardiac output where measured.

drugs.name: Adrenaline (epinephrine)
drugs.indications: Low cardiac output syndrome after cardiac surgery; anaphylaxis; cardiac arrest (with modified dosing after cardiac surgery)
drugs.adultDose: Infusion 0.01–0.2 mcg/kg/min. Arrest after cardiac surgery: CALS/STS advise against routine 1 mg boluses; if used, consider small doses (e.g. 50–100 mcg) only after shocks/pacing/resternotomy are being addressed.
drugs.preparationIndia: 1 mg/mL ampoules; common infusion 4 mg in 50 mL (80 mcg/mL).
drugs.cautions: Tachyarrhythmias, lactic acidosis (beta-2 effect), hyperglycaemia; rebound hypertension and graft/suture bleeding with bolus doses.
drugs.verify: Small-bolus dose in post-cardiac-surgery arrest varies between consensus documents; follow unit CALS protocol.

drugs.name: Vasopressin
drugs.indications: Vasoplegia after cardiopulmonary bypass refractory to noradrenaline
drugs.adultDose: 0.01–0.04 units/min IV infusion (fixed dose, not weight-based).
drugs.preparationIndia: 20 units/mL ampoules; 20 units in 50 mL = 0.4 units/mL (0.03 units/min = 4.5 mL/h).
drugs.cautions: Digital, mesenteric and coronary ischaemia at higher doses; hyponatraemia.

drugs.name: Methylene blue (methylthioninium chloride)
drugs.class: Guanylate cyclase / nitric oxide synthase inhibitor
drugs.indications: Rescue for catecholamine-refractory vasoplegia after cardiopulmonary bypass
drugs.adultDose: 1–2 mg/kg IV over 20–60 min; may be followed by an infusion in some protocols.
drugs.cautions: Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis) — relevant in India; serotonin syndrome with SSRIs/SNRIs/MAOIs/linezolid; falsely low SpO₂ readings; blue-green urine.
drugs.verify: Evidence is observational; confirm the cited EACTS/EACTA/EBCP CPB guideline wording on vasoplegia rescue; dose and use per cardiac anaesthesia consultant; check G6PD status if possible.

drugs.name: Dobutamine
drugs.indications: Low cardiac output syndrome after cardiac surgery
drugs.preparationIndia: 250 mg/20 mL ampoule; 250 mg in 50 mL = 5,000 mcg/mL.
drugs.cautions: Tachyarrhythmias, AF, hypotension from beta-2 vasodilation, myocardial oxygen demand.
drugs.monitoring: Heart rate and rhythm, cardiac index, lactate, ScvO₂.

drugs.name: Milrinone
drugs.indications: Low cardiac output with high SVR or pulmonary hypertension/RV dysfunction after cardiac surgery
drugs.adultDose: 0.125–0.5 mcg/kg/min IV; loading dose (50 mcg/kg) usually omitted because of hypotension.
drugs.preparationIndia: 10 mg/10 mL ampoule; 10 mg in 50 mL = 200 mcg/mL.
drugs.renalHepatic: Renally cleared: reduce in AKI (long half-life).

drugs.name: Amiodarone
drugs.indications: Post-operative AF (rhythm control or prophylaxis); VF/pVT after defibrillation
drugs.adultDose: AF: 150–300 mg (or 5 mg/kg) IV over 20–60 min, then 900 mg over 24 h (≤1.2 g/day). Arrest: 300 mg IV after the third shock (CALS: after three stacked shocks).
drugs.preparationIndia: 150 mg/3 mL ampoules; dilute in 5% dextrose; central line preferred for infusions >2 mg/mL.
drugs.cautions: Hypotension, bradycardia, QT prolongation, phlebitis; drug interactions (warfarin, digoxin).
drugs.monitoring: ECG, QTc, BP, LFTs and thyroid function with prolonged use.

drugs.name: Metoprolol
drugs.indications: Rate control and prevention of post-operative AF after cardiac surgery (if not hypotensive or low output)
drugs.adultDose: IV 2.5–5 mg over 2 min, repeat every 5 min to 15 mg. Oral 12.5–50 mg twice daily (restart early after cardiac surgery).
drugs.preparationIndia: Injection 1 mg/mL (5 mL); tablets 25/50 mg (tartrate) and extended-release succinate.
drugs.cautions: Hypotension, low cardiac output, bradycardia/heart block, bronchospasm.

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.indications: Symptomatic bradycardia (if no pacing wires or while setting up pacing)
drugs.adultDose: 0.5–1 mg IV, repeat every 3–5 min to a maximum of 3 mg.
drugs.cautions: Ineffective in denervated (transplanted) heart; tachycardia, urinary retention, delirium.

drugs.name: Isoprenaline (isoproterenol)
drugs.indications: Bradycardia/heart block when pacing is unavailable or failing; bridge to temporary pacing
drugs.adultDose: 0.5–10 mcg/min IV infusion titrated to heart rate.
drugs.preparationIndia: Ampoule strengths vary (e.g. 2 mg/mL or 0.2 mg/mL) — check label; e.g. 2 mg in 50 mL = 40 mcg/mL (1 mcg/min = 1.5 mL/h).
drugs.verify: Indian ampoule strength and supply vary; confirm before preparing.

drugs.name: Ondansetron
drugs.adultDose: 4 mg IV at end of surgery or for treatment; may repeat once after 6 h (use a different class if prophylaxis failed).
drugs.preparationIndia: 2 mg/mL ampoules; 4/8 mg tablets and orally disintegrating forms.

drugs.name: Paracetamol (acetaminophen)
drugs.adultDose: 1 g IV/PO every 6 h (max 4 g/day); 15 mg/kg if <50 kg; max 3 g/day in hepatic risk, malnutrition or chronic alcohol use.
drugs.preparationIndia: IV 1 g/100 mL bottles; 500/650 mg tablets.
drugs.renalHepatic: Reduce in hepatic impairment, low body weight.
drugs.cautions: Hepatotoxicity; IV dosing errors in low-weight patients.
